title: Rural-Urban Inequalities in Access to Early Childcare and Education and the Availability of Head Start Programs
abstract: Abstract Background The supply of early childcare and education (ECE) in the United States is insufficient compared to anticipated demand, with disparities in availability and features across communities. One of the core assumptions for federal funding for local Head Start programs is likely that these programs will alleviate a possible shortage of ECE in low-income and remote communities. While Head Start policy encourages strategically placing Head Start awards in potential supply-gap areas, it is unclear how Head Start programs can help address such supply gaps across geographic locations. Objective This study compares disparities in access to center-based ECE opportunities and examines the impact of public Head Start programs on improving access to ECE opportunities across rural-urban geographic locations, determined at the zip code tabulation area (ZCTA) level. Methods This study employs an ecological causal-comparative, or ex post facto, design to evaluate inequalities in access to ECE between rural and urban areas, using multiple data sources based on the state of Tennessee, including the American Community Survey (ACS), the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS), and federal Head Start websites. Results The finding indicates a significant difference in the demand: supply ratio across geographic locations. The finding also supports that rural areas had lower access to center-based ECE opportunities than urban areas. While descriptive statistics indicate unequal Head Start capacity, the analysis finds no substantial evidence of differential availability of Head Start slots and providers across geographic locations. Furthermore, the analysis of differences in demand: supply ratios with and without Head Start slot capacity also shows that the availability of Head Start slots significantly contributes to improving ECE capacity and reducing supply gaps (9% to 12%) across geographic locations. Conclusion The protective role of Head Start slots in reducing disparities in access also supports the need for increased federal funding to reduce geographic disparities in early learning opportunities and childcare infrastructure. These findings also support the need for ongoing or increased federal funding to reduce geographic disparities in ECE access, not just as an early learning intervention but also in policy discourse as a childcare equity and infrastructure program.
